scenes.title: Keys, Partitioning & Ordering
scenes.subtitle: How keys steer messages and preserve order
scenes.narration: Message keys decide which partition an event lands in, and that placement is what preserves ordering in Kafka.

scenes.title: The Role of the Key
bullets: A keyed message hashes to a fixed partition
All events for one key stay in order
Choose a key that groups related events
scenes.narration: When a message has a key, Kafka hashes it to select a partition, so every event with that key lands in the same partition. Because a partition preserves order, all events for one key are read in the order they were written. Messages without a key are spread round-robin across partitions for balance. The art is choosing a key that groups the events you need ordered together.

scenes.title: From Key to Partition
scenes.narration: Consider a producer that sets the key to user-42. Kafka computes a hash of that key. It then takes that hash modulo the number of partitions to pick a target. The event is appended to that partition, and every future event for user-42 follows the same path, guaranteeing their relative order.

scenes.text: Hot keys cause partition skew. If one key dominates traffic, its partition becomes a bottleneck no matter how many partitions you have.
scenes.narration: Watch out for hot keys, which cause partition skew. If a single key dominates traffic, its partition becomes a bottleneck no matter how many partitions the topic has.

scenes.title: Keying Messages
scenes.code:
# All events for a user land in the same partition
for event in events:
    producer.produce(
        topic='clicks',
        key=event['user_id'],   # ordering per user
        value=json.dumps(event),
    )
producer.flush()

# Changing partition count later re-maps keys
# and can break existing ordering!
scenes.narration: Here every event is keyed by user_id, so a single user's clicks stay ordered within one partition. Different users spread across partitions, giving parallelism without sacrificing per-user order. Be careful, though: increasing the partition count later changes the hash mapping. Existing keys may move to new partitions, which can break the ordering guarantee for in-flight data.

scenes.text: Key by the entity whose order matters, size partitions up front, and avoid changing partition counts on ordered topics.
scenes.narration: As a best practice, key by the entity whose order matters, size your partition count up front, and avoid changing partition counts on topics where ordering is important.
